Hostel warden's note, third-year block, October. Over the term I have watched Pooja step back from the corridor group that ranks everyone by phones and outings. In August she was at every one of their dinners. By October she sat with them only on Fridays. She began studying in the common room with Salma, who cares nothing for the group's ranking, and the two share a kettle and long evening walks. Pooja looked lonely in September, eating alone twice. Once I saw her stand at the group's door with a hand raised, then walk away. Rhea, who leads the group, sent a message: “We miss you.”

What I did next: I did not comment on the group. I asked Pooja whether the common room key for evenings would help. She said yes.

Saturday night. I did it again: skipped the rooftop thing with Meera's crowd. Nobody texted. That's the part that stings. Three months ago I checked my phone every ten minutes for their plans. Tonight I checked it just to see if anything was there, and it was empty. I ate dinner alone in the mess and hated it.

Then Uday messaged: “Dal-chawal at mine, come? No dress code, no ranking, lol.” I went. We watched an old film and argued about the ending, and I laughed until my ribs hurt. Nobody asked where my jacket was from.

I still miss the group a bit. But I slept better tonight than I have in weeks.
— Dilnaz

In the small college town of Bolpur, Anirban had ridden with the bike gang for two years. They owned the best motorbikes, sat on the college steps like kings, and judged everyone by their fathers' cars.
He started noticing how tired he felt after every evening with them. The same jokes. The same rankings.
One day he stayed back to watch the theatre group rehearse under the banyan tree. Sonali, who ran it, handed him a script. “We need someone to read the uncle's part. Only if you want.”
For the first month, the bike gang teased him and stopped calling. Evenings were long and quiet. He sometimes missed the roar of the bikes.
By winter, he was building sets, laughing at rehearsals, and nobody asked what his father drove.

qa.q: Where did the theatre group rehearse?
qa.a: Under the banyan tree.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel in the first month after leaving the bike gang?
qa.a: He felt lonely and a bit nostalgic, with long quiet evenings and missing the roar of the bikes.

qa.q: What made Anirban's move work over time?
qa.a: He kept going to the theatre group, where people valued his help rather than his status, until he felt he belonged.

qa.q: How might Sonali have seen Anirban at first?
qa.a: Sonali probably saw him as a curious outsider and invited him gently, without pressure.

grounding: Shows a young man gradually leaving a status-focused group for friends who value him without ranking, lonely first and steadier later.

At her university in São Paulo, Camila had been part of the “it” group since first year. They posted every outfit, judged every party, and dropped people who weren't cool enough.
She began to feel tired after every weekend. Her phone was full of photos and she couldn't remember one real conversation.
Priscila, from her statistics class, mentioned a volunteer choir at the community centre. Camila went, feeling silly.
The it-group noticed. “Choir? Seriously?” They stopped inviting her. For weeks, Friday nights were strange and empty. She scrolled through their photos, missing the noise.
By the end of the semester, she was singing alto next to Priscila, eating pão de queijo after practice, and her Fridays felt like hers.

qa.q: What part did Camila sing in the choir?
qa.a: She sang alto next to Priscila.

qa.q: How did Camila feel when the group stopped inviting her?
qa.a: She felt lonely and nostalgic, finding Friday nights strange and empty and missing the noise.

qa.q: What helped Camila find steadier belonging?
qa.a: Choosing a group built around a shared activity, the choir, where people valued her, and sticking with it through the lonely weeks.

qa.q: How might the it-group see Camila's choice?
qa.a: They seem to see it as uncool and a drop in status, which is why they mocked it and stopped inviting her.

grounding: Shows a young woman moving away from a status-focused group to friends who value her without ranking, lonely first and steadier later.

For two years Vinita had eaten dinner at the front table of the hostel mess: the girls who planned outfits for every fest and ranked everyone's internships. Lately, each dinner felt like an exam. "Only a state-bank internship?" Riya had said last week, laughing.
So in September Vinita began leaving early for the chess club in the common room. It was mostly quiet people: Pradeep, who played slowly and hummed; Anu, who brought peanuts for everyone. The first weeks were lonely. The front table stopped saving her seat. Some evenings she sat in her room scrolling through their photos, wondering if she'd made a mistake.
By November Pradeep had started saving her a board. Nobody asked about her internship. When she lost three games in a row, Anu just pushed the peanuts toward her. Walking back one night, Vinita noticed she hadn't checked her phone all evening.

qa.a: Anu brought peanuts for everyone.

qa.a: She kept turning up at the chess club week after week, which gave people like Pradeep and Anu time to make room for her.

qa.a: Pradeep probably sees a new regular worth welcoming, which is why he began saving her a board.
